title: Everyman
name: Everyman
description: Everyman (c. 1509-1519, Anonymous; England (from Dutch Elckerlijc)). God sends Death to summon Everyman to give account of his life. Fellowship, Kindred, and Goods all promise help but abandon him; only Good-Deeds, strengthened by penance through Knowledge and Confession, goes with him to the grave. Beauty, Strength, Discretion, and Five-Wits forsake him at the graveside. Everyman dies commending his soul to God, and the Doctor closes with the moral. Themes: Death and judgment; the vanity of worldly goods; good deeds as the only lasting wealth; penance and the sacraments. The most famous morality play in English; the complete text survives and is still performed worldwide.

key_points: Themes: Death and judgment; the vanity of worldly goods; good deeds as the only lasting wealth; penance and the sacraments
Note: The most famous morality play in English; the complete text survives and is still performed worldwide.

title: The Castle of Perseverance
name: The Castle of Perseverance
description: The Castle of Perseverance (c. 1400-1425, Anonymous; England (East Anglia)). The longest and earliest complete morality play: Mankind is born between a Good Angel and a Bad Angel, grows up, is tempted by the World, the Flesh, and the Devil with the Seven Deadly Sins, repents, and is besieged in the Castle of Perseverance by the vices. He falls again through Covetousness, dies unshriven, and is damned - though the play ends pleading God's mercy for all. Themes: The battle for the soul; the seven deadly sins vs. the virtues; deathbed repentance. Earliest surviving full-length morality play (3,649 lines); its staging diagram is the most detailed medieval stage plan in existence.

title: Mankind
name: Mankind
description: Mankind (c. 1470, Anonymous; England (East Anglia)). Mankind, a simple farmer, is counseled by Mercy to flee idleness, but the comic vices Mischief, Nowadays, New Guise, and Nought - led by the devil Titivillus - tempt him with scatological pranks and idle pastimes. After falling, Mankind despairs and nearly hangs himself before Mercy intervenes, teaching that despair is the unforgivable sin and leading him to repentance. Themes: Mercy vs. mischief; idleness as the root of sin; despair vs. hope; the power of repentance. Famous for its earthy comedy and the devil Titivillus, who collects idle syllables; a bridge between morality and Tudor interlude.

title: Wisdom (Wisdom Who Is Christ)
name: Wisdom (Wisdom Who Is Christ)
description: Wisdom (Wisdom Who Is Christ) (c. 1460-1463, Anonymous; England (East Anglia, Bury St Edmunds circle)). Wisdom (Christ) instructs the three faculties of the soul - Mind, Will, and Understanding - who are then seduced by Lucifer into pride and lechery, appearing in lavish worldly dress. After their fall into sin, Wisdom restores them through contrition, and the play ends in a dance symbolizing the soul's return to grace. Themes: The faculties of the soul; pride and spiritual corruption; restoration through grace; contemplative theology. The most theologically sophisticated morality play; its lavish staging directions suggest performance before a learned monastic audience.

title: The Pride of Life
name: The Pride of Life
description: The Pride of Life (c. 1350s (fragmentary), Anonymous; Ireland/England). Only about 500 lines survive: the King of Life boasts he fears neither man nor God, is challenged by Death, and the surviving fragment ends as the reckoning begins. A prologue warns that pride goes before a fall, and a king's messenger and a bishop debate the king's power. Themes: Pride as the root sin; death as the great leveler; the fall of the mighty. The earliest known morality play; though fragmentary, it establishes the genre's core allegory a half-century before Everyman.

title: Elckerlijc
name: Elckerlijc
description: Elckerlijc (c. 1495, Peter van Diest (attributed); The Netherlands (Dutch)). The Dutch original of Everyman: God complains of mankind's ingratitude and sends Death to summon Elckerlijc (Everyman). The same procession follows - fellowship, kin, and goods forsake him; good deeds, knowledge, and confession save him. Printed by 1495, it was translated into English as Everyman. Themes: Death and reckoning; the Dutch roots of the English morality tradition. The source play of Everyman; its discovery settled the long debate over which version came first.

title: Youth (The Interlude of Youth)
name: Youth (The Interlude of Youth)
description: Youth (The Interlude of Youth) (c. 1514-1520, Anonymous; England). Youth, full of pride and high spirits, rejects the counsel of Charity and falls in with Riot, who introduces him to Pride, Lechery, and the tavern life. After wasting his substance, Youth is confronted by Humility and repents, learning that youth's pleasures are fleeting and virtue is the only lasting company. Themes: Youthful folly vs. virtuous age; prodigality; the counsel of elders. A classic prodigal-son morality; its tavern scenes show the genre absorbing popular comedy.

title: Hickscorner
name: Hickscorner
description: Hickscorner (c. 1513, Anonymous; England). Freewill and Imagination abandon good counsel and fall in with the swaggering vice Hickscorner, who boasts, blusters, and leads them into theft and debauchery. Pity, Perseverance, and Contemplation eventually reclaim them, and Hickscorner is driven off - though he promises to return wherever idleness reigns. Themes: Free will and imagination corrupted; the swaggering Vice figure; perseverance in virtue. Gives the Vice his swaggering, boastful personality that Shakespeare's Falstaff and Iago would inherit.

title: Nature (Henry Medwall)
name: Nature (Henry Medwall)
description: Nature (Henry Medwall) (c. 1490-1500, Henry Medwall; England). Nature, God's deputy, divides man into body and soul, assigning Reason to govern the senses. Man, led by Sensuality and the World, squanders his gifts until Reason, with the help of Meekness and Understanding, reclaims him. The play ends with Nature's judgment on how each part of man was used. Themes: Body vs. soul; reason as governor; man's stewardship of creation. By Henry Medwall, chaplain to Cardinal Morton; one of the first English plays with a named, professional author.

t: Mundus et Infans (The World and the Child)
title: Mundus et Infans (The World and the Child)
name: Mundus et Infans (The World and the Child)
description: Mundus et Infans (The World and the Child) (1508 (printed), Anonymous; England). The World meets the newborn Child and renames him at each life stage - Wanton, Lust and Liking, Manhood, Shame, and finally Age. At each stage the World dresses him finer and leads him deeper into sin, until Age, broken and repentant, turns to Perseverance and is saved, showing life's full arc from innocence to redemption. Themes: The ages of man; the world as tempter; repentance in old age. A life-cycle morality covering birth to death; printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1508, among the earliest printed English plays.

title: The Play of the Weather
name: The Play of the Weather
description: The Play of the Weather (1533, John Heywood; England (court of Henry VIII)). Jupiter, annoyed by humanity's contradictory prayers about the weather, summons representatives - a gentleman, merchant, ranger, water-miller, windmiller, gentlewoman, laundress, and boy - each demanding different weather. Merry-report the Vice keeps chaotic order. Jupiter decrees the weather shall stay as it is, pleasing none and ruling all. Themes: Divine providence vs. human desire; social satire; the impossibility of pleasing everyone. Heywood's brilliant court interlude; a morality of cosmic order that doubles as Tudor social satire.

title: The Four PP
name: The Four PP
description: The Four PP (c. 1543-1547, John Heywood; England). A Palmer, a Pardoner, and a Pothecary compete in lying, each claiming the most outrageous marvels - the Pardoner with his fake relics, the Pothecary with his cures. A Pedlar judges their contest of lies, and the prize goes to the biggest liar. The play satirizes religious fraud and quack medicine with gleeful irreverence. Themes: Satire of religious corruption; the lying contest; Reformation-era skepticism. Heywood's masterpiece of comic debate; the lying contest is among the funniest scenes in early English drama.

Philologus, a scholar, is torn between Conscience and worldly advancement, vacillating between Protestant conviction and Catholic conformity under pressure. title: Enough Is as Good as a Feast

description: Enough Is as Good as a Feast (c. 1568, W. Wager; England). The Worldly Man hoards wealth with Covetousness while his tenants starve; God's Plague and Famine visit him, and on his deathbed he learns that enough is as good as a feast. His goods are divided, his soul is weighed, and the moral lands with proverbial force. Themes: Covetousness; the proverb as moral; deathbed reckoning. Built around its proverb-title; a plain, powerful sermon-play of the 1560s.

description: The Longer Thou Livest the More Fool Thou Art (c. 1568, W. Wager; England). Moros the fool, aged and unrepentant, is schooled by Discipline and mocked by the vices Impiety and Cruelty. title: The Tide Tarrieth No Man

description: The Tide Tarrieth No Man (c. 1576, Anonymous (Wager circle); England). Faithful Few, a sailor, must catch the tide - a figure for the fleeting opportunity of salvation - while the vices Greediness and Wastefulness delay and distract him. Christianity and Faith urge haste; the tide waits for no man, and the play's nautical allegory carries its urgency. Themes: Opportunity and delay; the seafaring life as spiritual allegory. A rare nautical morality; its tide metaphor gives the genre one of its most memorable titles.

title: The Nice Wanton
name: The Nice Wanton
description: The Nice Wanton (c. 1560, Anonymous; England). A mother's three children - Barnabas the obedient, Ismael, and Dalila the wanton - take different paths: Barnabas to virtue, the other two to whoredom, dicing, and ruin. Dalila dies of the pox unrepentant while Barnabas becomes a judge, staging a stark prodigal-children warning for parents. Themes: Parental counsel; prodigality; disease as moral consequence. A domestic morality of parenting; its frank treatment of vice shocked and fascinated Tudor audiences.

title: The Disobedient Child
name: The Disobedient Child
description: The Disobedient Child (c. 1560, Anonymous; England). A son defies his father's counsel, marries against advice, and reaps poverty, a shrewish wife, and misery - then repents and is reconciled. Satan and the vices gloat over his fall while Patience and Charity guide his return, making disobedience itself the allegorical antagonist. Themes: Filial obedience; the consequences of rash marriage; repentance and forgiveness. The disobedient-son plot that Shakespeare's audiences knew by heart; a staple of school and parish performance.

A contemplative morality closely related to Wisdom; its psychology of the soul fascinated medieval theologians.
